title: Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker, prep investigations into Trump's orbit
description: Democrats gave the official nod to Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Democrats are ramping up their plans to inve
body:
Democrats gave the official nod to Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Democrats are ramping up their plans to investigate the Trump administration come January.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  Democrats have been busy today on Capitol Hill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is one step closer to becoming the next speaker of the House after a vote behind closed doors this morning.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)HAKEEM JEFFRIES: The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable.PFEIFFER: And Democrats are previewing their investigation agenda for when they take over in January. NPR congressional correspondent Barbara Sprunt is at the Capitol and is with us on the line. Hi, Barbara.BARBARA SPRUNT, BYLINE: Hello.PFEIFFER: So it certainly appears that Hakeem Jeffries is the presumptive next speaker. But was this a unanimous vote?SPRUNT: It was not. There was some grumbling from newly elected progressive members who had said that they wanted to see new leadership. But Jeffries did run unopposed. This was an overwhelming vote of support for him. The vote was 251-11, and this sets him up for January, which is when the full House will vote for speaker.PFEIFFER: And on the Senate side, things are not looking as clear cut. The current minority leader is Chuck Schumer. He's being challenged by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen. What are their respective arguments for why they should get the top Senate job?SPRUNT: Well, some Schumer allies have been using a sports metaphor when talking about this. Like, if the manager brings a team to the World Series, why would they then fire him? You know, a lot of people see Schumer as instrumental in flipping nine Senate seats for Democrats, far beyond what many in the party even considered in their wildest dreams going into this election cycle. But Van Hollen argues voters made it clear that they want change, and he says that that extends to Democratic leadership. Progressives seem very excited about him, but zooming out, it was moderates and centrist Democrats who really opened up the map in big ways for Democrats this election cycle, particularly in the South. So there is this tension - right? - between the why switch horses midstream and the other side that says, well, the moment calls for shake-ups.PFEIFFER: And what's the general view on whether Van Hollen actually is a candidate who represents change?SPRUNT: Well, perhaps unsurprisingly, it depends on who you ask. You know, he calls himself an underdog. He's positioned himself as embracing the populist economic policies that really resonated with so many voters this cycle. And fairly early on, he joined calls to restrict arms sales to the Israeli government, which has certainly endeared him to a lot of progressives. He's been increasingly critical of the Democratic Party and the way that congressional leaders have historically approached the Trump administration. But others point out he's not really a generational-change candidate. He's 67 years old, about eight-ish years younger than Schumer. He represents a blue state. He's been in politics for decades. And in fact, he's already chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees, so he's not a new face.PFEIFFER: Barbara, in terms of the Democrats' agenda, since the election, they have been saying that they will aggressively conduct oversight of the Trump administration. Did they address that at all today?SPRUNT: They did, indeed. Congressman Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on oversight and the expected next chairman of the committee, sent a dozen letters to President Trump's allies and some family members telling them to hold on to their documents for upcoming investigations.PFEIFFER: Ah, sounds like a target list of sorts.SPRUNT: Exactly.PFEIFFER: Who's on that list?SPRUNT: Well, the president's two sons, his son-in-law, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, her adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President JD Vance. Those are just a few. Democrats' targets fall into four buckets broadly - alleged corruption within the Trump family, corporate corruption, misconduct in the Department of Homeland Security and what Democrats call the White House Epstein cover-up. Now, the White House has rejected those accusations of misconduct before and has warned Garcia that investigations could constitute a crime. That is something that legal experts push back on.PFEIFFER: Sounds like months and maybe years of coverage for you coming up.SPRUNT: (Laughter).PFEIFFER: That's NPR's Barbara Sprunt. Thank you.SPRUNT: Thank you.

title: Why the Nvidia scandal is a national security issue
description: The Nvidia scandal has spilled over into the Trump administration, which is now under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chip
body:
The Nvidia scandal has spilled over into the Trump administration, which is now under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  For more than two weeks now, the tech world has been consumed by the rolling crisis around Nvidia. The company's cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was pushed out after news reports of extramarital affairs that includes an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. The scandal has since spilled over into the Trump administration, and now it, too, is under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands. NPR's Ryan Lucas and Shannon Bond have been digging into this. Hey there.SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Hey there.RYAN LUCAS, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.DETROW: So the coverage so far has been about all the scandalous details of Huang's personal life, but this is a national security scandal. Tell us more about that.LUCAS: Well, right. And China, of course, is a superpower. It has the economic and military might that puts it almost on equal footing with the United States, and China and the U.S., of course, are in a race to develop artificial intelligence. And AI has implications in all facets of life, including cybersecurity, on the military battlefield and technological development in the economy. So the trickle-down effects of this are enormous. And so protecting the current American technological lead in AI is seen is very much a national security issue.BOND: And President Trump really sees this AI race with China as a binary win-lose situation. So here's how he described it back in September.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins.BOND: And look, Nvidia makes these chips that are really crucial to AI development. And so Jensen Huang has long argued that American companies should, in fact, sell these chips to China so that Chinese AI development is reliant on U.S. AI hardware. That view is not universally shared, including in the government, but it's one that Huang has really successfully pushed during this second Trump administration.DETROW: And this gets to an important factor here - the way that Huang's views have shaped administration policies.LUCAS: Well, look, the Biden administration took a hard line on this. It severely restricted the sale of the most advanced American AI chips to China to try to protect the U.S. national security and the country's technological edge in AI. Trump came into office in January of 2025, and things changed. Jensen Huang was actively lobbying the administration to loosen the restrictions. And for the past 18 months or so, America's most advanced AI chips, Nvidia chips, have been flying out the door to America's biggest rival, to China. I spoke to Chris McGuire about this. He worked on the national security council on AI and export controls. I asked him why China would want Nvidia's most advanced chips. Here's what he said.CHRIS MCGUIRE: These chips are the lifeblood of AI. They're the most important thing that you need for AI systems and AI development, and they're also the single biggest differentiator between the U.S. and China.LUCAS: Now, China can't make these top-end chips themselves, but despite the national security concerns, McGuire says over the last 18 months, some $60 billion in AI chips have gone to Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand legally. But those three countries can't support that level of AI buildout on their own. So some of those chips are suspected of having been smuggled into China. McGuire says the rest are in data centers that are primarily being used by China's top tech companies to train their own AI to make those models better. Here's McGuire again.MCGUIRE: The reason that this happened is that the Trump administration did not enforce the license requirement that would have applied to those countries, and it's just enabled a massive technology transfer out the door.LUCAS: Now, McGuire said this is potentially the biggest transfer of export control technology to an adversary in U.S. history, which, of course, begs the question of why and how that was allowed to happen. And there's an argument that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with Trump played a role here.DETROW: So what exactly did that relationship - that relationship between Trump and Huang - look like?BOND: Yeah. I mean, his profile was not this high at the beginning of Trump's second term. For example, he was not one of the tech CEOs who attended the inauguration, but Huang really successfully launched this campaign of personal diplomacy. And, Scott, as an example of just how close he became to President Trump, back in September, Huang was on stage at a big tech conference, and he took a call from Trump on his personal cellphone.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JENSEN HUANG: Mr. President, oh, yes, sir. I got to tell you something. I - if it wasn't because of you calling, I would - I'm on stage.BOND: He went on to put Trump on speakerphone and lavishly praised his leadership on AI. And you can really see how he's cultivated this relationship and has helped him become one of the most influential voices shaping the administration's AI policy. And Huang and others who share these views have framed making China dependent on American AI chips as a way for the U.S. to stay ahead in this AI race, which as I said, Trump really cares about.DETROW: So what actions has the administration taken that have benefited Nvidia?LUCAS: Well, the Trump administration has lifted restrictions on two specific Nvidia chips to allow them to be sold directly to China. The Trump administration also secured a massive deal to give the United Arab Emirates access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, a deal worth billions of dollars, and it did so despite concerns that those chips could end up, again, in China.Now, at the same time, I'm told that there was a recommendation in the summer of 2025 to impose an export license requirement to send AI chips to Malaysia and Thailand over the concerns that we have been talking about, but the Commerce Department sat on that. It didn't move forward. And so those chip sales - the chips that are at the very heart of the current scandal - those chip sales continued. And only this week, in response to this rolling scandal that we've seen, did the Commerce Department move to restrict those chip sales and close that loophole.DETROW: OK. So the Commerce Department made that move. Huang is out at Nvidia. What comes next?BOND: Well, Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer are set to answer questions from lawmakers on Capitol Hill. That'll start after Thanksgiving. Those lawmakers are going to have a lot of questions, you know, about this relationship, certainly, with the suspected Chinese spy, but also about these allegations, you know, that there may be ways in which they were evading export controls.Now, I should note, this week, Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and its compliance with export controls. You know, that's going to be a live issue. And, of course, Scott, Democrats are now going to be in control of Congress. So I think there is going to be more to come in terms of scrutiny and questions for Jensen Huang, but also for these administration officials and the decisions they made and what some of the thought process behind that and who might have been influencing that.DETROW: Yeah. That is NPR's Shannon Bond and Ryan Lucas. Thanks to both of you.LUCAS: Thank you.BOND: Thanks, Scott

title: The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?
description: It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connect
body:
It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connected to the convicted sex offender. His victims speak out.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:  Now we turn to an effort to shed light on the crimes of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, an effort that, in some cases, revictimized the women he abused. It's been a year since a new law required the Justice Department to release millions of files related to the Epstein investigation. But when the files were made public last year, so were the names and even phone numbers of some of the women he targeted. NPR's Ava Berger spoke with two Epstein survivors and to the sister-in-law of one survivor who died by suicide.ANNIE FARMER: My name's Annie Farmer. I was 16 years old when I was abused by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.DANI BENSKY: My name is Dani Bensky, and I was 17 years old when I met Jeffrey Epstein.AMANDA ROBERTS: My name is Amanda Roberts, and I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, and I am the sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, one of the most prominent survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.FARMER: There has been so much that's happened in the last 12 months and, really, in the lead-up, you know, to the passing of the legislation, as well - was very busy and very chaotic.BENSKY: I keep thinking about that day. We sat in the gallery of the House, and we got to watch the votes come in. And it was so surreal to sit there and just watch the board and watch everything start to flip to yes. We went from that moment, and, you know, tears were streaming as we passed this new law.ROBERTS: There was this feeling of we knew the pain that each other carried. And there was this moment of unity, and it was that feeling, that unity, that courage, together, that drove this entire year.FARMER: The moment of joy that comes to mind for me from this year was actually the day that the files were released. I think that there - as more people in the public have become aware of both the extent of the crimes and also the amount of information that was gathered by the government about those crimes, there has been a sense of validation.BENSKY: But then I did find my name in a memo pad. It certainly wasn't redacted, as it had my phone number in it. And we started to see that the perpetrators were really being protected, and we couldn't find perpetrators' names and predators' names, but we could certainly find a lot of victims' and survivors' names. And so that felt really awful.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)BENSKY: There are a thousand girls, more than a thousand girls and women that have been abused in those files. And so, yeah, you might be talking about some powerful people, but you're also talking about over a thousand lives that have been completely derailed.ROBERTS: There is such an appetite for justice in this community, in our country right now that I believe if we just keep this momentum pushing forward, we will see real accountability for all abusers out there. And we can really see a societal shift that says it doesn't matter what power and position and money you have, we are all to be held accountable to the same laws and rules.FARMER: I certainly hope that there's a future where I never have to speak the names Epstein and Maxwell. I think many, many survivors in this case are interested in their lives moving on and not having to look so much in the rearview mirror about, you know, what's happened here.ROBERTS: If Virginia was here to see this, I would tell her that I'm so proud (crying) and that I wish that you would have held on just a little bit longer to see this. But I understand why she felt like she couldn't, because she had been failed by every single system in her life.PFEIFFER: Virginia Roberts Giuffre was one of Epstein's most outspoken accusers. She died by suicide last year. That was Dani Bensky, Annie Farmer and Amanda Roberts speaking with NPR's Ava Berger on the one-year anniversary of the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.And if you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
description: Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., appears at
body:
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., appears at a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 13, 2023. On Wednesday, he released document preservation letters that lay the groundwork for incoming investigations into the Trump family and its allies.
                
                    Drew Angerer/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Drew Angerer/Getty Images
    

   
   The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.   "Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."    The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."    
   "Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.   The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.    In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."    "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."   Here's a closer look at the letters Garcia sent:    Donald Trump Jr. — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, and the financing of his wedding after-party by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.  President Trump later told reporters the costs for the wedding celebration was later paid back. "You have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father's presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people," the letter reads.  Eric Trump — "pay to play" allegations and potential conflicts of interest, his stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture. "Oversight Democrats have found that your roles as a co-founder of World Liberty Financial and a key player in the Trump family's pay-to-play schemes have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years," said the letter. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law — allegations of conflicts of interest, his investment firm Affinity Partners, and using his government role to enrich himself and his companies. "Directly or indirectly, you have received billions of dollars in fees and investments with particularly troubling ties to Middle East states where you also have a government role," the letter reads. "This raises urgent questions about transparency, conflicts of interest, and the abuse of what appears to clearly be a government position—with influence over war, peace, and nuclear proliferation as well as direct access to President Trump—for personal profit." Former Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle. She was previously engaged to Trump Jr., and was contacted by Garcia over allegations of pay-to-play schemes. "As ambassador, you appear to have been intent on leveraging your position to cash-in," said the letter.  Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend — construction and donations for the White House ballroom, financed in part via private donations to the Trust.  White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — allegations of abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement under his direction. "Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the 'linchpin' and 'architect' of the Trump Administration's most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties," reads the letter. "We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses."Former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski — allegations of abuse of DHS funds, corruption and self-dealing. Vice President J.D. Vance — allegations of secret meetings inside the White House Situation Room about the administration's handling of the Epstein files. "Reportedly, you were even the first to suggest that Ghislaine Maxwell be interviewed in hopes of using her testimony to distance President Trump from Epstein, despite President Trump's well-documented decades-long friendship with the notorious abuser and sex-trafficker," the letter reads. "These discussions appear to be directly linked to an apparent quid pro quo in which Maxwell was moved to a minimum-security prison camp after she made favorable statements about President Trump in a highly unusual prison interview conducted by then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche." Former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — allegations of secret White House meetings surrounding the Epstein investigation. "Reporting describes you as refusing to release documents concerning allegations against President Trump to the public," the letter said.  Attorney General Todd Blanche — allegations of a cover-up of the Epstein files, failure to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and the decision to transfer Maxwell to a minimum-security prison. "You have refused to cooperate with our investigation, or to fulfill your legal responsibilities to be transparent with the Committee and the American people," the letter said. "This obstruction is even more concerning given your direct involvement in the broader cover-up, as well as your history as President Trump's personal attorney." Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Federal Prison Camp Bryan Warden Tanisha Hall — regarding Maxwell's transfer to a minimum-security prison camp days after she was questioned about Trump and his relationship to Epstein. "Committee Democrats will not tolerate the Administration's refusal to respond to our inquiries and, in the future, will not hesitate to compel information from individuals enabling the cover-up of Maxwell's and Epstein's crimes," the letter said.

title: Democratic strategists think Montana House race could hold the secret to future wins
description: Montana is sending a Democrat to the U.S. House for the first time in three decades. Many in the party think Sam Forstag's campaign may be a pl
body:
Montana is sending a Democrat to the U.S. House for the first time in three decades. Many in the party think Sam Forstag's campaign may be a playbook for how Democrats can win again in rural America.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Montana last sent a Democrat to the U.S. House 32 years ago. That's the same year Montana's newest representative, Sam Forstag, was born. The former firefighter is now on Capitol Hill for freshman orientation, and his rise is giving Democrats a potential roadmap for competing in rural America. NPR's Kirk Siegler reports.KIRK SIEGLER, BYLINE: Montana has been solid Trump country since he was first elected president in 2016, and until the evening of November 3, it seemed like Democrats here could never figure out how to respond to his popularity.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)SAM FORSTAG: (Inaudible).(CHEERING)SIEGLER: All that changed in dramatic fashion as Sam Forstag declared victory before a boisterous crowd of mostly young voters in the liberal college town of Missoula.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)FORSTAG: We can again be a state that bends the course of this country's history for the better. The only way we fix this is we send working-class people to Washington so that we can go fight for ourselves.(CHEERING)SIEGLER: Montana hasn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. House for three decades. It's also been 10 years since any Democrat here won a statewide race. In the crowd, Whitney Williams sees his win as a sign that Democrats shouldn't write off rural America.WHITNEY WILLIAMS: Democrats didn't do a good enough job with rural America, there's no question. But I think that that's changing, and I think it's changing pretty dramatically, and we can see it in these numbers tonight.SIEGLER: How did he pull it off? Forstag didn't shy away from ripping on President Trump, casting him as a corrupt billionaire gutting public lands protections and public services. But he also blasted Democrats, saying he made barely 19 bucks an hour jumping out of airplanes into wildfires during the Biden administration. The day after the election, Forstag, in jeans and a Carhartt jacket, stood out in Missoula's freezing fog, holding what he said was his first-ever official press conference.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)FORSTAG: Quite frankly, I don't care what party you're in. I just care that you're going to be out there working for working people.SIEGLER: He said working people too many times to count.In this huge district, from Glacier National Park to Yellowstone, people drive pickups to work and are fuming over high gas prices. And the national parks and federal lands agencies gutted by Trump's DOGE didn't sit well in tourism-dependent Montana either. Professor Lee Banville is a political analyst for Montana Public Radio.LEE BANVILLE: He really has kind of laser-focused in on this message of, you know, it's not about turning Montana blue. It's about turning Montana blue collar.SIEGLER: Banville thinks it's too early to tell whether Forstag will serve as a model for rural Democrats or if he just ran at the right time. The handsome former smokejumper was all over social media, looking rugged chic, working in the woods and blasting Trump for cutting hundreds of vital federal jobs here.BANVILLE: In some ways, you know, kind of like Talarico, kind of like Ossoff, he's kind of made for TikTok. He's very quotable. He's running his campaign both as a broad effort but also as a real soundbite machine.SIEGLER: Republican state legislator David Bedey says there just wasn't as much enthusiasm for Forstag's opponent, conservative radio host Aaron Flint. Bedey says Trump's policies like tariffs and the Iran war may have alienated some Montanans who voted for him in 2024.DAVE BEDEY: I think it was largely the moment, but I'm going to give Forstag credit. He ran a great campaign. It's amazing how many people are fed up with both parties.SIEGLER: Before Trump, Montana was famous for split-ticket voters. Whitney Williams says Forstag's win is a sign that's possible again. Her dad, the late Montana congressman Pat Williams, was the last Democrat to win this district.WILLIAMS: Montanans like voting for people who are authentic and honest. And they're working people. And I think that we Democrats have fielded extraordinary candidates around this country.SIEGLER: Now voters here say those candidates must actually deliver for working people, many of whom appear to have soured on the president and his MAGA movement.Kirk Siegler, NPR News, Missoula, Montana.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon
description: Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon   In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black wome
body:
Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon   In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black women who were all elected in the 2026 midterms.

    
        State Government
    


      
            
                  
            November 18, 20264:51 PM ET
         
      
       From
   
   
                              By                
            


      
      Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon.
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6043103/nx-s1-10010445" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black women who were all elected in the 2026 midterms.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Next year, Black women from the Democratic Party will be leading most government agencies in Georgia alongside the first ever Black woman elected governor anywhere in the U.S. DorMiya Vance with WABE reports on what the new leadership means for Black women.DORMIYA VANCE, BYLINE: Georgia voters made it clear they wanted to see a change in who represents them next year.MAUI BIGELOW: Every time there's a fire, y'all call Black women.VANCE: Maui Bigelow (ph) cast her ballot in a south Atlanta suburb on Election Day. She said it was a pivotal moment to get more Black women into state government. That night, Democrats swept offices and celebrated historic wins. In Georgia, every state government office on the ballot went to Democrats. And Black women now hold eight of those 10 positions, including attorney general, secretary of state and, of course, governor.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS: Thank you, Georgia. I am honored to be your 84th governor.VANCE: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson, becoming the country's first-ever Black woman elected governor. She didn't emphasize her identity in her campaign. Still, voters were ready to give new candidates a chance, says Tammy Greer, a political scientist at Georgia State University.TAMMY GREER: So the political environment happened. These women had the audacity to come forward. And they were able to get their message to translate across demographics.VANCE: And when the state legislature convenes next year, Georgia will also have more Black women representatives. Greer says such prominence is new.GREER: For so long, Black women have been in the background who have pushed others ahead of themselves while doing all the work.VANCE: The governor is pretty powerful in Georgia. Bottoms can appoint and fill thousands of positions in state government. And she'll have a say over the state budget. Bottoms will have an ally leading the statehouse because Democrats won the majority there. Carolyn Hugley has been a state representative for over 30 years. She's nominated to become speaker of the House. She'd be Georgia's first Black woman in that role. She says this incoming class of Black women will be judged under a microscope.CAROLYN HUGLEY: Sometimes people have unrealistic expectations of African American women in particular.VANCE: She says she has dealt with prejudice and judgment throughout her career, including comments about her hairstyles and her clothes. And she expects harsh criticism ahead.HUGLEY: That has always been a part of being a Black woman in America. And this is not new territory for me. I've been a Black woman for a long time.VANCE: Hugley says, based on her experience, it's crucial that new leaders stay focused on their responsibilities as elected officials and not be distracted by any unreasonable backlash.For NPR News, I'm DorMiya Vance in Atlanta.(SOUNDBITE OF GLADYS KNIGHT AND THE PIPS SONG, "MIDNIGHT TRAIN TO GEORGIA")

title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
description: President Donald Trump, right, Chinese P
body:
President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China.
                
                    Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP
    

   
   SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.   "History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."   Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."   
   "In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.   Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:   Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.   There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.   In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.   Summit speed dating   Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.   
   Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.   Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.   "Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.   "We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."   Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."   Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.   Getting there    The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.   For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.   Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.   Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.   Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.   Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.   
   Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.   The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.   Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.   A new Yalta?   From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.   In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.   Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.   Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.   The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.   Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.   Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.   Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.   
   Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."   It was hard to see why.   Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.   The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.   Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
description: Families look on as President Donald Tru
body:
Families look on as President Donald Trump speaks during a ceremony to sign the "Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act" in the East Room of the White House on July 16, 2025.
                
                    Evan Vucci/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Evan Vucci/AP
    

   
   When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.   
   But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.    "The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.     Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.   
   What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.    "Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."   Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths   According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said.  By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.   
   Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.   "It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.   Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.   
   Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Joe Biden met China's President President Xi Jinping in Woodside, Calif., in November 2023, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperative conference. China agreed to curtail shipments of the chemicals used to make fentanyl, the drug at the heart of the U.S. overdose epidemic.
                
                    Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times
    

   
   The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.   Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.    White House on Biden role in declines   NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden.  In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.   "While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.    
   Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."    According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.   "We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated  operations," she said.   
   But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.   
   "I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."   Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.   Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.     The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.   "Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

schema.headline: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
description: Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a
body:
Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference in the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.   Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.   "Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy  is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.    
   Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.    "Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.    The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.   Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.   It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.   
   While Jeffries will still have to navigate intraparty divides, the size of Democrats' majority affords him room to weather some dissent.   He's faced resistance from some within the party's left-most flank, who argue Democrats should prioritize advancing a more progressive agenda next year, lobbying for votes on Medicare for All and legislation that would stop the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel.    Among those who voted against Jeffries were a number of newly-elected members — some who won with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America. In a statement after the vote, they said they have engaged in "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries to secure commitments on their policy priorities.    "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."   Among those who signed the statement were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York;  New Jersey's Adam Hamawy; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Colorado's Melat Kiros; Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.   After the vote, Jeffries told reporters "the results of today's election speak for themselves."    "We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism — not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people."     Given that Democrats will hold double digit margins in the chamber — an edge propelled by the success of more moderate candidates in districts President Trump carried in 2024 — it's unclear how much leverage the left wing of the party will have in the speaker's vote.   Divides inside the party may prove more pronounced in the Senate, where some Democrats are more publicly questioning whether current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is best suited to deliver on voter demands for change.   
   Schumer faces a challenge from Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy last week and is pitching himself as an alternative to the status quo, echoing much of the progressive populist messaging that several successful Senate candidates ran on this cycle. Like Schumer, Van Hollen has also served in Congress for decades.    Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate for nearly a decade, contends that he still has the needed votes to be elected majority leader. However, Van Hollen's challenge comes as a handful of current and incoming members have declined to back Schumer for the job.   Both sides still have time to shore up votes, with leadership elections set for early December.

schema.headline: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
